title: Sulayman Pasha returns to Acre; Jazzar welcomes him 'like a lost son'
why: Reconciles Jazzar with the mamluk rebel of 1789 who would later succeed him. Sources disagree between 1801 and 1802.
cite: Wikipedia 'Jazzar Pasha' says 1802; 'Sulayman Pasha al-Adil' says 1801 (rev 1377827500)
note: year differs between two Wikipedia articles

title: Jazzar besieges Jaffa until Abu Maraq flees
why: Jazzar defied a firman branding him rebel; he later bought back imperial favour at Constantinople.
cite: Wikipedia 'Jazzar Pasha' (rev 1371729075), 1801-03 section

title: Ottomans make Jazzar wali of Damascus after Wahhabi seizure of Mecca
why: The Porte replaced Abdullah Pasha, who had failed the hajj caravan, with the Acre governor; Jazzar's Kurdish units held Damascus.
cite: Wikipedia 'Jazzar Pasha' (rev 1371729075)

title: Jazzar falls ill with tertian fever; Sulayman leads the hajj caravan
why: Illness left Jazzar inactive and made Sulayman Pasha de facto heir in the hajj role of 1803-04.
cite: Wikipedia 'Jazzar Pasha' (rev 1371729075)

title: Porte secretly names Ibrahim Pasha Qataraghasi governor of Sidon and Damascus
why: Appointed as Jazzar's illness became grave, to avert a succession fight in Acre.
cite: Wikipedia 'Jazzar Pasha' (rev 1371729075)

title: Jazzar Pasha dies in Acre
why: Ended a 28-year rule of Sidon Eyalet; refines the existing April 1804 entry with a day-level date from Wikipedia.
cite: Wikipedia 'Jazzar Pasha' (rev 1371729075): 'died on 7 May 1804'
dup_of: Jazzar Pasha dies; Sulayman Pasha later governs Sidon

title: Isma'il seizes Acre; Porte brands him a rebel and Ibrahim Pasha besieges
why: A prisoner freed by soldiers took power after Jazzar's death; Sulayman Pasha joined the siege on return from the hajj.
cite: Wikipedia 'Jazzar Pasha' (rev 1371729075) and 'Sulayman Pasha al-Adil' (rev 1377827500)

title: Ibrahim Pasha leaves siege for hajj caravan; Sulayman commands at Acre
why: Sulayman was then made wali of Sidon, giving him strong reason to finish Isma'il.
cite: Wikipedia 'Sulayman Pasha al-Adil' (rev 1377827500)

title: Sulayman disbands Albanian guard; 1,000-2,000 troops remain
why: Acre's cotton wealth was shrinking; Sulayman ruled by diplomacy with a small army of about 200 in Acre itself.
cite: Wikipedia 'Sulayman Pasha al-Adil' (rev 1377827500)

title: Sulayman buys hundreds of mamluks, swelling his force to about 2,500
why: Bought after Muhammad Ali's 1811 massacre in Egypt, as grain sales to England filled the Acre treasury.
cite: Wikipedia 'Sulayman Pasha al-Adil' (rev 1377827500): summer 1812

title: Silahdar Sulayman Pasha replaces Sulayman as governor of Damascus
why: Sulayman al-Adil kept Sidon, enlarged with Tripoli Eyalet and Latakia; he twice more served briefly as Damascus governor.
cite: Wikipedia 'Sulayman Pasha al-Adil' (rev 1377827500)

title: Sulayman builds watchtowers along main roads of Sidon Eyalet
why: Part of his road-security policy; the roads themselves stayed in disrepair.
cite: Wikipedia 'Sulayman Pasha al-Adil' (rev 1377827500)

title: Haim Farhi has Abu-Nabbut removed from Jaffa to clear Abdullah's path
why: Removal of Jazzar's last senior mamluk left no domestic rival to Farhi's candidate.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abdullah Pasha of Acre' (rev 1344770354)

title: Sulayman Pasha dies and is buried beside Jazzar in Acre
why: Last of the mamluk governors of Sidon; he left no male heir.
cite: Wikipedia 'Sulayman Pasha al-Adil' (rev 1377827500)

title: Porte confirms Abdullah Pasha as wali of Sidon after Farhi's bribes
why: Farhi lobbied five months; bribes in Constantinople reached about 11 million piastres. Bashir kept order meanwhile.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abdullah Pasha of Acre' (rev 1344770354): 'On 27 January 1820'

title: Abdullah Pasha has patron Haim Farhi strangled
why: The Jewish financial adviser who installed him was killed after a quarrel; the Farhi family later helped move the Porte against Abdullah.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abdullah Pasha of Acre' (rev 1344770354): 'On that same night, 8 August 1820'

title: Porte orders Abdullah to fortify coast, disarm Christians
why: The Morea uprising and Russian tension made Abdullah see only Bashir as able to do it, so he sought Bashir's return.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649), section Suppression of Maronite risings

title: Abdullah demands 1.1 million dirhams from Hasan and Salman Shihab
why: An impossible levy; with Bashir's allies undermining them, the two Rashayya emirs agreed to step down.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Bashir enters Jezzine; Druze 'uqqal mediate the Shihab succession
why: Mediation by Druze religious leaders led Hasan and Salman to concede before the 17 May 1820 accord.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Bashir enlists Abu Nakad sheikhs to crush the northern Maronite rising
why: His Druze fighters forced Jubail, Bsharri and Batroun to submit; Abu Khattar al-Aynturini led the delegates.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Lehfed rebels demand tax equality; Shia gather at Ras Mishmish
why: Delegates (wukala) from each village; historian William Harris calls it the first peasant articulation of identity and autonomy.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649), quoting William Harris

title: Darwish Pasha's Beqaa deputy raids 'Aammiq, triggering war with Acre
why: Bashir tried to mediate; Abdullah refused Damascus's offer to cede the Beqaa and asked Bashir to take it instead.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Darwish Pasha's forces lose in Anti-Lebanon and Hauran to Bashir and Abdullah
why: Khalil Shihab, Bashir's son, had been made mutasallim of the Beqaa; Yazbaki Druze fought with Damascus.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Porte decree dismisses Bashir; Mustafa Pasha sent to Damascus
why: The Porte, alarmed by the Acre-Lebanon action against Damascus, sent an emissary to Mount Lebanon.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Battle of Mezzeh: Abdullah and Bashir rout Darwish Pasha outside Damascus
why: Bashir mustered 12,000 men and Abdullah 4,000; about 1,200 of Darwish's troops died against 40 on the winning side.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abdullah Pasha of Acre' (rev 1344770354)

title: Darwish Pasha besieges Acre with Mustafa and Bahram Pashas
why: Backed by Salamun Farhi's money; Abdullah held with about 2,000 men. After five months Darwish was dismissed.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abdullah Pasha of Acre' (rev 1344770354)

title: Foreshocks begin the Aleppo-Antioch earthquake sequence
why: The last big foreshock came half an hour before the 13 August mainshock; seismicity then ran for over two years.
cite: Wikipedia '1822 Aleppo earthquake' (rev 1366163891)

title: Magnitude 7 Aleppo earthquake felt on Lebanese coast
why: Estimated 20,000 dead (30,000-60,000 reported); maximum intensity IX at Jisr al-Shughur; may have raised a tsunami.
cite: Wikipedia '1822 Aleppo earthquake' (rev 1366163891)
dup_of: Aleppo-Antioch earthquake, felt along the Lebanese coast

title: Most destructive aftershock of the Aleppo earthquake
why: Aftershocks continued for about two and a half years across northern Syria.
cite: Wikipedia '1822 Aleppo earthquake' (rev 1366163891)

title: Muhammad Ali gets Abdullah pardoned and Acre siege lifted
why: Mustafa Pasha was sent back to Aleppo; the Janissary-linked Farhi network was already falling from favour.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abdullah Pasha of Acre' (rev 1344770354): April 1823
note: Wikipedia's Bashir article says March 1822; the Abdullah article gives April 1823. The existing hub entry uses 1822-03.

title: Hesekiel al-Baghdadi and his brother Ezra executed in Constantinople
why: The banker who had arranged Abdullah's 1820 appointment fell as the Porte moved against the Janissary-linked financiers.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abdullah Pasha of Acre' (rev 1344770354)

title: Porte fines Abdullah 25,000 purses and strips Tripoli, Latakia, Gaza, Jaffa
why: He passed the whole fine to Sheikh Bashir Jumblatt; Emir Bashir cut Jumblatt's share to a third.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abdullah Pasha of Acre' (rev 1344770354)

title: Porte restores Gaza and Jaffa to Abdullah Pasha
why: Part of the post-siege settlement, as he paid the fine imposed in 1823.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abdullah Pasha of Acre' (rev 1344770354)

title: Tripoli revolt against caretaker governor when Sulayman Bey al-Azm leaves for hajj
why: Partisans of Mustafa Agha Barbar led it; Abdullah, whose reach had been cut, made Barbar stop from Beirut.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abdullah Pasha of Acre' (rev 1344770354)

title: Sheikh Bashir enters Beiteddine with 7,000 men; mediation fails
why: He and Ali Imad, Arslans, Khazens and anti-Bashir Shihabs allied to force Emir Bashir to reconcile over the unpaid million piastres.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Abdullah sends 500 Albanian irregulars to Bashir; Moukhtara routed days later
why: Reinforcement turned the 28 December loss; Jumblatt and Imad fled to the Hauran.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Ali Imad executed; Damascus hands Sheikh Bashir to Acre
why: Captured by Damascus forces after the Moukhtara defeat; Imad was summarily executed.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Bashir razes Jumblatt and Imad houses; Druze flee to Hauran
why: He redistributed Chouf, Kharrub, Tuffah, Jezzine and Beqaa districts to his son Khalil, the Talhuqs and the Abu Nakads.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)
dup_of: Jumblatt tax districts redistributed to Shihab, Talhuq and Abu Nakad

title: Bashir turns to Maronite clergy as his main administrators until 1840
why: Patriarch Yusuf Hubaysh welcomed the shift; Druze muqata'jis became resentful, deepening Druze-Maronite tension.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649), 'Centralization and shift to Maronite clergy'

title: Porte restores Tripoli to Abdullah; he replaces Ali Agha with Barbar
why: Believed Abdullah could restore order in an unruly district.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abdullah Pasha of Acre' (rev 1344770354)

title: Porte gives Abdullah the districts of Jerusalem, Nablus and Hebron
why: Taken from Damascus Eyalet because its governor could not collect the hajj tax; Ottomans feared a Muhammad Ali invasion.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abdullah Pasha of Acre' (rev 1344770354)

title: Abdullah and Bashir besiege Sanur fortress of the Jarrar sheikhs
why: The fortress held three months and fell in March 1831; Abdullah then reconciled with the Nablus sheikhs.
cite: Wikipedia 'Abdullah Pasha of Acre' (rev 1344770354)

title: Bashir hires Jirji Baz as mudabbir, replacing the Dahdah clan
why: Part of the Bashir-Baz deal, sworn on both the Quran and the Gospel, without Jazzar's knowledge.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Imad-led Yazbakis back rival Shihab emirs against Bashir
why: Jazzar supported the Yazbaki faction for four years until most Druze sheikhs condemned the Imads in 1803.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Druze take Jubail after Baz's killing; Yusuf's sons blinded
why: Bashir then sent loyalty assurances to the governors of Tripoli and Sidon. (corrected from 1807-05: Wikipedia has Baz ambushed and strangled on 15 May 1807 and Druze partisans killing his brother at Jubail; type was massacre, deaths 1 (Baz's brother))
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Bashir levies two years' jizya and kharaj in advance on Maronite peasants
why: Applied to Matn, Keserwan, Batroun and Jubail, sparing Druze muqata'jis, to pay Abdullah's 1 million dirhams; trigger of the ammiya.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Bashir pledges 4,000 fighters to Muhammad Ali in return for support
why: Muhammad Ali's backing for Bashir and Abdullah was his path to hegemony in Ottoman Syria. Bashir's exile in Egypt began 1821.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649)

title: Bashir demands 1 million piasters from Jumblatt; Jumblatt chooses Hauran exile
why: Sheikh Bashir had defected in 1821; from the Hauran he began preparing for war with Emir Bashir.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bashir Shihab II' (rev 1375192649); year approximate (after Bashir's return)

title: Fisk and Jonas King leave Jerusalem to spend summer on Mount Lebanon
why: The two American Board missionaries headed north to learn Arabic and survey Syria before choosing a permanent station.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.314

title: Fisk sails from Jaffa to Acre, lodging with the English agent
why: He met a Catholic priest defending papal infallibility; the journey north set out the coast route to Beirut.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.315

title: Fisk and King reach Sidon, put up with the English agent
why: Population of Sidon was put at 4,000 to 6,000, Tyre at 1,000 to 3,000, both loose estimates. They met LJS missionary Lewis.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.316

title: Pliny Fisk reaches Beirut, first American Protestant base in Syria
why: He judged Beirut best station: Lebanon retreat for summer, consuls, sea links; Jessup gives the same date.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.317
dup_of: Isaac Bird and William Goodell found the first permanent American mission station in Beirut

title: Fisk finds Beirut population estimates range from 3,000 to 14,000
why: He judged the lowest figure nearest the truth; Goodell called it the emporium of all that dwell upon the mountains.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.318

title: American missionaries lodge at Antoura, former Jesuit college
why: Rev. Mr Way occupied the building; Fisk made it his summer base and Jonas King went to Deir al-Qamar.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.321

title: Fisk visits Mar Hanna Shuwayr, Greek Catholic convent with Arabic printing press
why: 30 to 40 monks printed Psalters, Gospels and prayer books by hand; Fisk noted users wanted large type.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.322

title: Fisk and Wolff visit the abandoned convent of Hindiyya near Antoura
why: Volney had told her story; priests would not discuss it. Fisk heard she died a few years before at Aleppo.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.324

title: William Jowett of Church Missionary Society arrives in Beirut
why: Fisk rode in to greet him; a week of joint talks at Antoura followed, 23 to 29 September, on mission method.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.326

title: Fisk visits Bzommar, Armenian Catholic patriarch's seminary of about 20 students
why: Studies were grammar, rhetoric, logic, metaphysics and theology; the monks asked what a printing press would cost.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.326

title: Syrian Catholic patriarch Peter Jarwy succeeds an aged predecessor at Sharfeh
why: The 73-year-old former patriarch had resigned a few years earlier; Jarwy had just come back from Europe.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.325

title: Fisk and companions sell or give 23 Scriptures at Batroun
why: The Maronite priest Istafan hosted them; callers said English visitors usually asked only for wine and good food.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.327

title: Tripoli judged to hold about 15,000 inhabitants, mostly Muslims
why: Fisk's estimate, lodged with the English vice consul.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.327

title: Fisk visits Kannoubine, seat of the Maronite patriarch
why: He counted about 100 convents in Mount Lebanon, 60 to 70 of them Maronite, and put the population at 100,000 to 150,000.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.328

title: Fisk counts 389 trees in the Cedars grove; King counts 321
why: He measured the largest at over 40 feet round; earlier authors had said 5, 15, 20 or 28 cedars.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.329
note: King's count is read from OCR 'o21', taken as 321

title: Fisk finds two feet of snow on Lebanon summit in October
why: Tested the claim that snow lies year-round; he suspected sailors mistook white rock for snow.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.331

title: Baalbek's young emir seats his uncle in chains after a staged peace
why: Fisk witnessed the pomp of reconciliation; Baalbek had about 200 dwellings, mostly Matawila, few Greek Catholic families.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.333

title: Zahle reported to hold about 1,000 families, mostly Christian
why: Fisk reached it after a night in the rain; next day he visited the Syrian Catholic patriarch at Mar Ephraim.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.334

title: Fisk finds patriarch Peter Jarwy hostile to Bible societies
why: Jarwy had toured England raising funds said to be for Scriptures on Lebanon, but opposed missionaries.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.334

title: Fisk sells 400 Psalters in Beirut to a Catholic who resells them
why: The Psalter was the universal school book among Syrian Christians, so it sold best.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.334

title: Fisk and Jowett leave Beirut for Jerusalem via Nabi Yunus
why: They slept at a guest house built by Emir Bashir for travellers, kept by a Turkish dervish.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.336

title: Fisk and King visit Emir Bashir, get travel letter
why: Bashir let them travel and reside in the mountains to learn Arabic; Fisk noted he was the first reigning Christian emir.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.319

title: Deir al-Qamar counted at 3,000-4,000 fighting men
why: Fisk called it the mountain capital and the only Lebanese place where Turks or Jews lived; the emir palace stood an hour beyond.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.319

title: Fisk calls Bashir 'almost a king' under Acre pasha
why: The emir, he wrote, ruled Druze and Christians; most mountain people were Maronite, many Druze, very few Muslims.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.320

title: Qozhaya monks print Syriac and Karshuni; few can read
why: Maronite monks printed and bound their church books; Fisk saw only church lessons, no complete Bible.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.328

title: Fisk visits Kraim and Ain Waraqa convent colleges
why: Fisk found Italian and Latin books and four folio volumes of papal bulls; Syriac and Arabic were taught at Ain Waraqa.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.334

title: Fisk sees siege damage at Jazzar Mosque, Acre
why: Walls and cloister had been seriously hit during the 1822-23 siege of Acre.
cite: Bond, Memoir of the Rev. Pliny Fisk (Boston 1828), p.338

title: Goodell and Bird families sail from Malta for Beirut
why: They took passage on the Maltese brig La Divina Providenza, bound for Cyprus and Beirut, meaning first to reach Jerusalem.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.76

title: Greek privateer stops brig carrying American missionaries off Beirut
why: The Greek war at sea reached Syrian waters; the vessel then anchored four miles from Beirut and the missionaries landed next day.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.78

title: Goodell and Bird families land at Beirut, carried ashore through the surf
why: No wharf existed; the British consul Abbott lodged them. His was the only English family in town and had the only glazed window.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.79

title: Maronite patriarch's order read in Beirut church bans missionaries' Scriptures
why: It told people to return or burn English-printed editions; the papal vicar-general told Goodell and Bird he had not authorised it.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.87

title: Emir Bashir camps near Beirut with troops; aims unclear to residents
why: Goodell wrote it was a secret whether he would help Greeks, Turks, or take the city himself; gates stayed shut.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.89

title: Acre pasha's Albanians and Bedouins plunder Beirut outskirts after Greeks leave
why: A French merchant lost about 5,000 Spanish dollars; Bedouins cut down Goodell's door. Many residents fled to the mountain.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.89

title: Beirut gardens left uncultivated as silk season nears and owners hide
why: The Kehya Bey sequestered abandoned property and extorted those who came out; Bird's house sheltered all missionaries in Syria.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.91

title: Two months of beatings and forced payments by Acre troops in Beirut
why: Goodell describes people condemned without trial and beaten to raise levies; by 19 May he judged the storm spent.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.91

title: Abdullah Pasha orders payment of 2,875 piastres to Goodell after a painting
why: A Greek artist's picture of Bedouins in Turkish uniform breaking in persuaded the pasha, who said his men did it.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.92

title: Mission runs 13 schools with about 700 pupils, over 100 girls
why: By the end of 1826 the schools marked a change in attitudes to girls' education, as Goodell wrote, despite the Greek raid.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.93

title: Maronite bishop's plan to bar landlords from renting to missionaries fails
why: The Greek attack made the bishop flee and several best Maronite houses were offered to the mission instead.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.93

title: Mission's first Arab and local converts join communion at Beirut
why: Dionysius Carabet, Gregory Wortabet and Mrs Maria Abbott, wife of the British consul, were received; Asaad Shidyaq was prayed for in prison.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.94

title: Church order read in Beirut bans dealing with missionaries
why: Nobody was to speak to them, enter their houses, serve them, buy or sell; Latin and Greek churches proclaimed the same ban around 14 January; another Greek-church blast followed on 28 January, similar to the Maronite one.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.95

title: Eli Smith, Gobat, Kugler and Nicolayson join Beirut communion
why: Sixteen people from four continents and nine churches attended the monthly concert; Smith had just arrived in Syria.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.96

title: Plague breaks out at Beirut, pausing the persecution of missionaries
why: Panic suspended the church ban and let people visit the missionaries' houses; plague returned early in 1828.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.98

title: News of Navarino reaches Beirut; Franks flee the city
why: Goodell's family fled by night to Mansouriyeh; the Muslim population's reaction to the destruction of the Turkish fleet was feared.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.101

title: Fear of Muhammad Ali invasion and European intervention in Greece unsettles Beirut
why: Frankish residents left; native Christians fled to the mountains; Goodell moved his family to the Maronite convent of Der Kalaat.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.99

title: Goodell and Bird families return to Beirut after five months apart
why: They hoped to resume work, but consular protection was about to end.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.103

title: American mission families sail from Beirut to Malta
why: Authorities long withheld leave; Jessup dates Bird's return to May 1830, ending the two-year absence.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.103

title: Goodell records Asaad Shidyaq twice escaped, then was seized by the patriarch
why: He was kept chained; the date and manner of his death were unknown to the missionaries.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.98

title: Goodell family settles in rented house outside Beirut
why: A wealthy Turk's house a mile from the landing became a Bible depot visited by all faiths.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.80

title: Bird arrested in Jerusalem, returns to Beirut in May
why: Beirut, under British protection and growing trade, became the mission's headquarters because Jerusalem was disturbed.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.85

title: Greek fleet lands 500 men at Beirut, repelled
why: Twelve ships then bombarded for 90 minutes. Goodell counts 4-5 Greeks and nearly 20 Turks killed.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.88
dup_of: Greek flotilla raids Beirut, briefly holds a seafront quarter

title: French warships evacuate consul and subjects from Beirut
why: Consular protection ended as the powers and the Porte moved toward war; plague reappeared the same year.
cite: Goodell memoirs, Forty Years in the Turkish Empire (Boston 1876), p.103

title: Yusuf Pasha's army sacks Tripoli, stripping iron and marble
why: Burckhardt: his troops took even pavements; Mustafa Agha Barbar held the castle. Dating is from the siege that ended in February 1809.
cite: Burckhardt, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (London 1822), p.171
note: year inferred from siege ending Feb 1809

title: Barbar quits Tripoli castle for Acre after five-month siege
why: Sulayman Pasha interceded; Yusuf Pasha granted honours of war and bought the castle's remaining provisions.
cite: Burckhardt, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (London 1822), p.171

title: Sulayman Pasha of Acre also invested with Tripoli pashalik
why: Burckhardt lists Tripoli's governors; Sulayman held Tripoli in 1810 and Damascus in the same period, with Barbar as deputy.
cite: Burckhardt, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (London 1822), p.171

title: Emir Bashir joins Sulayman's army to depose Yusuf Pasha of Damascus
why: He took 400 firelock men from Zahle. Burckhardt's account differs from the Wahhabi-threat story told in other sources of 1810.
cite: Burckhardt, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (London 1822), p.7
note: conflicts with entry on 1810 mobilisation at Tiberias against Wahhabis

title: Sulayman gives Bashir the Bekaa and 100 purses for backing against Damascus
why: The Bekaa came under Bashir's command when Sulayman took Damascus in 1810; Damascus and Mount Lebanon long disputed its villages.
cite: Burckhardt, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (London 1822), p.194

title: Djahdjah Harfush returns as emir of Baalbek after brother Sultan flees
why: More than 15 Harfush family members had died in the brothers' feud; Bashir gained 15 purses a year from Baalbek.
cite: Burckhardt, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (London 1822), p.11

title: Zahle runs more than 20 indigo dye houses and weaves cotton cloth
why: Burckhardt also reports 30 percent interest rates and most sales on credit; cotton came from Safad and Nablus.
cite: Burckhardt, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (London 1822), p.7

title: Maronite patriarch resides at Kannoubine again, first in long time
why: Harassment by Matawila on the Baalbek road had made earlier patriarchs abandon it; peasants hang silkworm bags before saints' icons there.
cite: Burckhardt, Travels in Syria and the Holy Land (London 1822), p.21

title: Press at Qozhaya near Ehden prints Syriac prayer books

title: Batroun has 300-400 houses, run by Emirs Qadan and Melhem

title: Abd al-Ahad and Jirjis Baz recalled killed together on the emir's orders

title: Bzommar Armenian Catholic convent, built for 15,000 pounds

title: Deir al-Qamar has 900 Maronite, 300 Druze, 15-20 Turkish families

title: Kesrouan iron ore smelted at Nebae el Mauradj

title: Silk growers pay 20-25 percent tax; grain farmers over 50

title: Ain Warka Maronite school teaches 16 poor boys
why: Grammar, logic, philosophy and Syriac; the bishop was adding a dormitory. Boys had to take orders on leaving.

title: Kesrouan makes 60 kantars of silk; extortions of 5-6 miris

title: Asaad Shidyaq leaves Beirut bishop to serve Emir Hasan Shihab as clerk

title: Patriarch Yohanna al-Hilu shelters Asaad, then dismisses him at Bashir's request

title: Bashir's mountain army defeats Damascus troops at the city walls

title: Asaad Shidyaq reaches new Patriarch Yusuf Hubaysh, recently elected

title: Asaad compiles a book of Maronite church law for Hubaysh

why: Bird says four Americans, Fisk, King, Goodell and himself, were then distributing Bibles in Lebanon; the reply fell to Asaad to answer.

title: Asaad Shidyaq is introduced to American missionaries in Beirut as Arabic teacher

title: Jowett lands at Beirut; British consul Peter Abbott receives him

title: Yusuf Hubaysh elected Maronite patriarch over Bishop Hanna Maroni

title: Convent of Harissa shelters Emir Bashir's former opponents, now fined

title: Deir al-Qamar holds about 2,000 inhabitants; Beiteddine palace employs 2,000
